questions.q: Write the negation of the statement: "All squares are rectangles." Express your answer in a complete sentence.
questions.a: The negation is: "Not all squares are rectangles" or equivalently "There exists at least one square that is not a rectangle." A wrong answer like "No squares are rectangles" reveals the student incorrectly negated the universal quantifier by changing 'all' to 'none' instead of 'not all' / 'there exists ... not'.

questions.q: If p is the statement "2 + 2 = 5", what is the truth value of ∼p? Explain why.
questions.a: p is false (since 2+2=4), therefore ∼p is true. A wrong answer stating ∼p is false reveals the student thinks negation preserves truth value or confuses the statement's content with its truth value.

questions.q: Write the negation of the compound statement: "The number x is even and x is greater than 10." Use De Morgan's law conceptually.
questions.a: The negation is: "The number x is not even OR x is not greater than 10" (i.e., x is odd or x ≤ 10). A wrong answer "x is not even and x is not greater than 10" reveals the student did not switch 'and' to 'or' when negating a conjunction.

questions.q: Consider the statement: "For every real number x, x^2 ≥ 0." Write its negation and determine whether the negation is true or false.
questions.a: Negation: "There exists a real number x such that x^2 < 0." This negation is false because the original statement is true (square of any real number is non-negative). A wrong answer like "For every real number x, x^2 < 0" reveals the student negated the predicate but kept the universal quantifier.

questions.q: A student writes the negation of "Some integers are negative" as "Some integers are not negative." Is this correct? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, it is incorrect. "Some integers are negative" means "There exists an integer that is negative." Its negation is "No integer is negative" or "All integers are non-negative." The student's answer is actually the negation of "All integers are negative." This reveals confusion between 'some' (existential) and 'all' (universal) quantifiers.

questions.q: Create a statement p such that both p and ∼p are false in the real world, or explain why this is impossible.
questions.a: It is impossible. By definition of negation, p and ∼p always have opposite truth values; one must be true and the other false. A student who tries to create such an example reveals they do not grasp the law of excluded middle or think truth values depend on external facts rather than logical structure.
